blocks.text: 1. Compression
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163455-797425305.png
Compression addresses a storage cost first raised back in the Embeddings module: how to store vectors more efficiently without losing too much accuracy.
It shrinks how much space each stored vector actually takes up, trading a bit of precision for significant storage savings.
2. The Storage Cost Recap
Storing millions of full precision vectors adds up to a large amount of raw storage, as the dimension-count math in Embedding Dimensions already showed.
Across replicated and sharded systems that cost multiplies further, since each shard and each replica needs its own copy of every vector.

blocks.content: {"headers":["System factor","Effect on storage"],"rows":[["Sharding","Splits data, but total storage stays the same overall"],["Replication","Multiplies total storage by the number of replicas"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Reducing Precision Per Dimension
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163456-356532701.png
Each dimension does not need full precision to remain useful for comparison.
Storing fewer bits per number shrinks the vector while keeping its overall shape roughly intact.
4. Quantization Explained
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163457-457679139.png
Quantization rounds each dimension's value down to a smaller set of possible levels.
That trades a small amount of precision for a large reduction in storage size.
5. Dimensionality Reduction Recap
Reducing the number of dimensions, as covered in Embedding Dimensions, is another, complementary way to shrink storage.
Combining fewer dimensions with fewer bits per dimension compounds the savings.
6. Accuracy Loss From Compression
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163458-36845941.png
Every compression technique gives up some precision in exchange for smaller storage.
Measuring that accuracy loss, using the same techniques covered in Embedding Evaluation, confirms whether the tradeoff was worth it.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Applying aggressive quantization without measuring the resulting retrieval quality risks silently degrading a pipeline's accuracy well below an acceptable threshold, unnoticed until users start complaining.

blocks.text: 7. Compression And Search Speed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163458-64578703.png
A smaller vector also compares faster, not just stores more compactly.
Compression often improves both storage footprint and query speed together.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A compressed vector requires fewer arithmetic operations to compare against a query vector, so compression can speed up search throughput in addition to reducing storage footprint.

blocks.text: 8. When To Compress And When Not

blocks.alt: When To Compress And When Not
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163459-384879885.png
A small collection rarely justifies the added complexity of compression.
A massive collection, on the other hand, often makes compression an easy, worthwhile tradeoff.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Collection scale","Compression decision"],"rows":[["Small","Complexity rarely justified by the modest storage savings"],["Massive","Storage and speed gains typically outweigh the accuracy tradeoff"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Compression Is Worth Applying

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Compression Is Worth Applying
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163459-872293911.png
Very large collections at scale benefit most from compression.
Small collections where accuracy matters most may prefer full precision vectors instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below quantizes a full precision vector and measures the resulting storage savings.

code.content:
import random

def generate_fake_vector(dimensions):
    return [random.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(dimensions)]

def quantize_vector(vector, levels=16):
    # rounds each value down to one of a fixed number of levels
    return [round((v + 1) / 2 * (levels - 1)) for v in vector]

full_precision_vector = generate_fake_vector(128)
quantized_vector = quantize_vector(full_precision_vector)

full_precision_bytes = len(full_precision_vector) * 4  # 32 bit floats
quantized_bytes = len(quantized_vector) * 0.5  # roughly 4 bits per value at 16 levels

print(f"Full precision vector: {full_precision_bytes} bytes")
print(f"Quantized vector: {quantized_bytes} bytes")
print(f"Storage reduction: {(1 - quantized_bytes / full_precision_bytes) * 100:.1f}%")

print(f"\nFirst 5 original values: {[round(v, 3) for v in full_precision_vector[:5]]}")
print(f"First 5 quantized values: {quantized_vector[:5]}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the quantized vector taking a fraction of the storage of the full precision original, at the cost of rounding each value to a coarser set of levels.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Applying aggressive compression without measuring the resulting retrieval accuracy loss.
Compressing a small collection where the storage savings do not justify the added complexity.
Assuming compression always hurts speed, when it often improves comparison speed too.
Forgetting that dimensionality reduction and quantization are two complementary, compounding levers.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Compression shrinks how much space each stored vector actually takes up.
Storage costs multiply further across replicated and sharded systems.
Each dimension does not need full precision to remain useful for comparison.
Quantization rounds each dimension's value down to a smaller set of possible levels.
Dimensionality reduction and quantization are complementary techniques that compound savings.
Every compression technique trades some accuracy for smaller storage, which should be measured.
Smaller, compressed vectors often compare faster, improving query speed alongside storage.
Small collections rarely justify compression's complexity; massive collections often do.
